The midterm election delivered a considerably stronger Democratic showing than the market was anticipating. Democrats captured both the House and Senate, with gains extending well beyond the traditional battlegrounds and into states and districts that had been reliably Republican. The result is a genuine blue wave and, from the market's perspective, the important issue this morning isn't politics -- it's surprise. Markets can discount good news and bad news; what they have a more difficult time discounting is an outcome that wasn't fully anticipated.

Historically, that reduction in legislative flexibility has not necessarily been a negative for stocks. Markets generally prefer predictability, and divided government can make sweeping changes in taxes, spending and regulation more difficult to enact. Fidelity's research makes an important point: historically, the market's post-election behavior has been driven less by which political party won than by the reduction in uncertainty once the election was over. As Fidelity puts it, the environment doesn't necessarily become completely clear - it simply becomes “less unclear.” And this is where the historical picture becomes particularly interesting.

Since 1938, the S&P 500 has been higher 95% of the time during the 12 months following a midterm election, with an average gain of approximately 14%. Fidelity's longer-term work on the presidential cycle also shows the post-midterm year as historically the strongest portion of the four-year election cycle. Schwab finds a similar pattern: since 1974, the S&P 500 has averaged a 5.7% gain in the three months following midterms and 12.4% over the following six months.

That historical tendency is reinforced by seasonality. We have now entered what has traditionally been the strongest six-month period of the year, November through April. Since 1945, the S&P 500 has averaged roughly 7% during that six-month stretch versus just over 2% from May through October. November itself has historically been one of the market's strongest months, and the November through January period has also been particularly favorable

So we now have several potentially favorable historical forces beginning to converge: the election is behind us, political uncertainty has been reduced, Washington is moving toward divided government, we're entering the historically strongest part of the presidential cycle, and we're simultaneously moving into one of the strongest seasonal periods of the year.

That does not mean the market has to go straight up from here. In fact, given the magnitude of the election surprise, some additional volatility would not be unusual. The market still has to digest what the Democratic Congress could mean for taxes, regulation, AI infrastructure, energy policy and other areas. More importantly, the election doesn't make the other risks disappear. The 10-year Treasury yield remains near 5%, oil remains above $100, inflation and Fed policy remain significant issues, and questions surrounding AI valuations and capital spending are still very much in play. Those fundamental forces ultimately matter more than the election itself.

What matters now is whether the tape begins to confirm the historical script. I want to see the major indexes absorb the election shock and hold support, but even more important, I want to see improvement beneath the surface: broader participation, expanding leadership, more stocks reclaiming key moving averages, fewer new lows, more quality setups and, ultimately, breakouts that can gain traction and hold their gains.

Encouragingly, breadth has already improved, with nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks moving above their 10-week averages after starting the month at only about 20%.

The bottom line is that the election result may have been more dramatic than investors expected, and the market's initial volatility reflects that surprise. But the election also removes a major uncertainty, creates divided government and places us directly into a historically favorable post-midterm and seasonal window. If the market needs to shake out further in the near term, I would not automatically interpret that as bearish. It could be part of the process of discounting the new political reality and establishing a more durable low.

Of course, the historical and seasonal backdrop doesn't guarantee the outcome. Stock setups will be our main focus. In the meantime, our shorts act as a hedge, and as always, our longs are protected with stops.

With millions of people on Twitter, every day someone makes a prediction or a “market call.”  And out of all those people, every day SOMEONE is going to be right.
It’s like the lottery. Every week there’s a winner—but every week the name is different.
I’ve been succeeding in the stock market for 43 years. Not because I was a natural-born trader, and certainly not because I can predict the future. It’s the result of practice, study, discipline, patience, strategy, rules, experience—and being smart enough to never allow a prediction to get in the way of my respect for risk.
My entire fortune has been built on three key rules:
1. I never buy at the bottom.
2. I always sell too soon.
3. I never hold or add to losses.
That’s how you survive long enough to build a generational fortune. And for those smart enough to heed its wisdom, this tweet is worth a fortune.

A person comes to me with a spark.
I fan that spark until it becomes a flame.
I feed the flame until it becomes a fire.
I fuel the fire until it becomes a roaring blaze.
And once that fire is burning from within, they no longer need me to keep it alive.
That is the essence of great coaching. It's not about creating the spark. It's about recognizing what's already inside someone and helping them turn it into something unstoppable.
But there's a requirement.
The student must come with two things: a spark and an empty cup.
The spark is the desire, the hunger, the willingness to do whatever it takes.
The empty cup is the humility to put aside what you think you know, open your mind, and make room for new wisdom.
I can fan a spark. I can fuel a fire. I can fill an empty cup with knowledge earned through decades of experience. But I cannot ignite a fire in someone who has no desire to burn. And I cannot pour wisdom into a cup that is already full.
If you have no spark, or you are uncoached, there is nothing I can do for you except wish you luck.
The first few lines are taken from my favorite coach of all time, Cus D'Amato. A man who understood how to make a champion. RIP

UPDATE: On October 15, I added the $SPY short to our portfolio in anticipation of a general market decline. At the time, the position was initiated as a hedge against our long exposure.
Since then, the market declined, with the $QQQ falling 11% and the $SPY declining 5% from our entry price (short). That weakness stopped us out of all but one of our long positions ($TEVA) - either at small losses or with profits on stocks where we had backstopped gains.
By default, as our long exposure came down, the $SPY short transitioned from being a hedge to leaving us net short the market.
We view the recent action as a stealth bear market in certain areas, where the major indexes have masked significant deterioration beneath the surface, particularly among AI infrastructure and technology stocks. Many of those names have suffered substantial declines from their highs, driving them to oversold levels.
My original stop on the $SPY was 778.00, which represented a new all-time high only about 1% above our short price. I have now improved that stop to our breakeven price of 769.64, eliminating stop-loss risk on the position.
The trade has already been a success from a risk/reward standpoint. We initially risked approximately 1%, while the $SPY declined roughly 5% from our entry—about a 5R move.
Our decision to hold for a potentially larger move was based first on the position serving as a hedge and, subsequently, on our ability to de-risk the trade to the point where we now have zero principal risk.
This is a classic way I approach many of my market/ETF trades when shorting the general market.

When I make a trade, my thinking is never about being right or even wrong. It's about risk vs. reward. I call it Bell Curve Thinking. I ask myself, if I make this trade 1000 times, does it come out a winner. Is it likely that the trade's upside is at least 2-3X the my stop?  If I get those right, the rest takes care of itself.
My most recent $SPY short is a perfect example. The stock fell 5X my stop. I had the opportunity to capture 5Rs. But that's precisely what afforded me to hold for a bigger move while improving my stop to breakeven. I made that decision based on the odds at the time.  If I turn out to be wrong... nothing lost. Next.

My memo to our clients this morning:

Yesterday, we doubled our already profitable S&P 500 short exposure because we believe the potential for further downside remains worth the miniscule risk we are taking. Our original position has been completely de-risked, and the additional shares were added using what we call an "add and reduce" technique", allowing us to increase exposure without materially increasing overall risk. This puts us in our favorite position: large profit potential with very small risk.

The Nasdaq triggered a follow-through day. We take that seriously, but now we need to see whether the rally can gain traction or if distribution rears its head in the coming days. With a good-sized hedge bet in place, we are open to adding some longs as they meet our criteria. Currently, the list is small, but there are a few names we are considering. Refer to our Focus List for current names.

Many of yesterday's biggest winners were in the AI/technology stocks that had been beaten down and severely oversold. CoreWeave is an especially good illustration. It exploded 24.7% yesterday, but closed at $60.77 versus a 52-week high of $138.2 - still down about 56% below its high. IREN gained 5.6% but closed at $20.84 against a $70.71 high, still roughly 71% below its high. Those are enormous rallies but occurring inside badly damaged charts. Most of yesterday's tech stock rallies occurred within strong downtrends.

Macro and policy risks still argue for staying selective rather than chasing a market with very few sound stock setups. Sticky inflation, the prospect of additional Fed rate hikes, rising long-term interest rates, and increasing talk of regulation surrounding AI and data centers are all reasons to remain cautious about a nascent rally that, so far, has largely been a rebound from an oversold condition.

Interest rates remain particularly important. After pulling back from an overbought condition, the 10-year yield has started turning higher again, while the 1-year yield jumped sharply. That is not exactly the backdrop you want to see if you’re looking for expanding equity valuations and a sustained risk-on move.

Investors Intelligence bulls fell sharply to 37.0% from 42.6% last week, the lowest bullish reading since early April, when bulls reached 33.3%. That's a significant reversal from just six weeks ago, when bulls stood at 57.7% as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were hitting highs. That peak was one of three readings above the 55% danger level that historically signals elevated risk.

At the same time, bears jumped to 24.1% from 18.5%, the highest bearish reading since April. The shift is encouraging from a contrary-sentiment standpoint, particularly after several weeks when bearish readings remained unusually low.

Sentiment is definitely moving in the right direction, but we don't believe the ratio of bulls to bears has reached the extreme normally associated with a major contrary buy signal. For now, we view the change primarily as a directional indication. Optimism is being wrung out and pessimism is building as stocks retreat from their highs. That's constructive, but it isn't necessarily capitulation. We would like to see sentiment deteriorate further before treating it as a powerful contrary signal.

The fourth quarter, particularly November and December, is historically one of the strongest periods of the year for stocks. But 2018 is a good reminder that seasonality doesn't always win out, especially when the Fed is tightening and the market is already showing signs of deterioration.

In 2018, the Fed was already raising interest rates when the market started to come under pressure. The S&P 500 broke below its 50-day moving average and sold off hard in October. It then snapped back roughly 8%, which at the time looked like the correction might be running its course, particularly with the market heading into the seasonally strong November-December period.

But the rally failed.

The S&P rolled over and fell another roughly 16% before finally bottoming on Christmas Eve. From the September high to the December low, the decline was nearly 20%.

The point is not that 2018 is going to repeat itself. It's that you can't assume the market is going higher simply because you're entering a historically strong seasonal period. When the Fed is tightening, rates are rising and market conditions are deteriorating, those forces can overwhelm seasonality.

We always respect seasonal tendencies, but we don't trade the calendar. We trade the market in front of us. Price and volume, breadth, leadership, interest rates and, most importantly, the action of individual stocks will tell us whether the market is actually improving.

2018 is a good example of why you have to keep an open mind. Even during one of the strongest seasonal periods of the year, the market can still go down.

Why?

Because an impending push up is growing likely.

Based on history, the current bull market is long in the tooth; the fifth longest on record. However, since 1950 the S&P 500 has never declined in the year after mid-terms elections. The average S&P 500 gain in pre-election years is 17.2%. What is noteworthy is: most of the gains have come in the first half of pre-election years. The S&P 500 has been flat-to-down in the second half (see chart).

We are heading into a period with multiple bullish tendencies working in the market’s favor. Year-end seasonality is one.  The historically strong first half of the Presidential cycle is another (see charts).

If we can get through this period without the Fed moving into a fast tightening cycle, those tailwinds should remain intact. Under that scenario, I would expect the current correction to be relatively short-lived and ultimately give way to a resumption of the broader uptrend.

Could we bottom soon?

There is an interesting historical precedent worth keeping in mind as we approach Thursday's scheduled meeting between the U.S., Russia and China. Going back to some of the most significant meetings between the world's major powers, the stock market was higher following nearly every one of them—sometimes substantially higher.

In 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta. Stocks rallied immediately following the meeting and continued higher over the next several weeks.

In 1972, Nixon's historic meeting with Mao in China was also followed by a rising market and new highs in the weeks that followed.

The Reagan-Gorbachev summits show a similar pattern. Following Geneva in November 1985, stocks moved higher.

Reykjavik in October 1986 actually ended without an agreement, yet the market shrugged off the disappointment and gained roughly 5% over the next three weeks.

Following the Washington summit in December 1987, where Reagan and Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty, the market rallied sharply, gaining roughly 7% within a week and continuing higher.

After their Moscow summit in 1988, stocks again rallied strongly, gaining roughly 7% over the next couple of weeks and close to 10% within a month.

Obviously, this is a small sample and every period had a different economic and market backdrop. But the pattern is noteworthy: these major superpower meetings were generally followed by higher stock prices over the ensuing days and weeks.

That matters to us because we're currently short the S&P 500 and sitting on a profitable trade. If the market gives us additional downside going into Thursday, I will likely use that weakness to cover some or potentially all of our short exposure ahead of the meeting.

There's enough historical precedent for a positive reaction that I don't see a reason to overstay a profitable short going into the event.

I have not made the decision to cover my shorts just yet, but a decline from here could be just the opportunity to cover right into weakness at peak equity.

Some Color Through the Minervini Lens
Subject: $SPY, $DIA short positions initiated on 10/15 and doubled on 11/11.

I’m now sitting on a 5R profit relative to my original risk, meaning I’ve made five times what I initially risked. That great for two reasons: 1. I've made a worthwhile gain. 2. It opens up options.
I can simply take the profit. 5-to-1 reward-to-risk is an excellent trade and certainly well worth the effort.
Or I can move my stop to breakeven, give the position some room, and play it for a potentially much bigger move, having open-ended profit potential with zero risk.
That's exactly where I am now. The profit I've built allowed me to move my stop to breakeven and effectively eliminate the original risk. I've earned the right to play for the bigger move, working my way into the best situation possible; a profitable freeroll.
And that's the key. I don't enter a trade and immediately decide that I'm going to hold out for some pre-determined target or enormous move regardless of what happens. First, the trade has to prove itself. If it moves sufficiently in my favor and gives me an opportunity to de-risk the position, then I can decide whether to take the profit or give it time to develop into something more.
That's how you put yourself in position for asymmetric leverage: start with small risk, let the trade earn its way, improve your worst-case scenario, eliminate the risk when the opportunity presents itself, and then give the bigger move a chance to happen risk free.
Of course, at that point, you always have the option of taking a 5R profit, and that in itself can make you rich.
Best wishes, and best of luck.

I’m now sitting on a 5R profit relative to my original risk, meaning I’ve made five times what I initially risked. That great for two reasons: 1. I've made a worthwhile gain. 2. It opens up options.
I can simply take the profit. 5-to-1 reward-to-risk is an excellent trade and certainly well worth the effort.
Or I can move my stop to breakeven, give the position some room, and play it for a potentially much bigger move, having open-ended profit potential with zero risk.
That's exactly where I am now. The profit I've built allowed me to move my stop to breakeven and effectively eliminate the original risk. I've earned the right to play for the bigger move, working my way into the best situation possible; a profitable freeroll.
And that's the key. I don't enter a trade and immediately decide that I'm going to hold out for some pre-determined target or enormous move regardless of what happens. First, the trade has to prove itself. If it moves sufficiently in my favor and gives me an opportunity to de-risk the position, then I can decide whether to take the profit or give it time to develop into something more.
That's how you put yourself in position for asymmetric leverage: start with small risk, let the trade earn its way, improve your worst-case scenario, eliminate the risk when the opportunity presents itself, and then give the bigger move a chance to happen risk free.
Of course, at that point, you always have the option of taking a 5R profit, and that in itself can make you rich.
Best wishes, and best of luck.

This morning’s rally may look impressive, but this is exactly why I covered the shorts. The market had gotten oversold enough to produce a rip-your-face-off rally. After capturing nearly 7R on the downside, there was no reason to overstay the trade.
That said, keep this morning’s action in perspective. A number of stocks are up a whopping 10%-30%, but most are barely a blip on the charts. For now, they’re counter-trend rallies in stocks that are still in significant downtrends, particularly in Technology.
The S&P 500 fell 11.6% from its October 6 record high, the first 10% correction since the February-April 2025 selloff, but we are not out of the woods. There’s still work to do before we can say an effective bottom is in place. One strong day doesn’t suddenly create a new uptrend.
For now, I expect volatility to remain elevated. Enjoy the rally, but keep it in context. The market still has to prove itself. Prepare for backing and filling, and even lower lows in the major indexes before this correction is over.
The tricky thing about an oversold market is that it can always get more oversold. And even after momentum bottoms, price can still go on to make lower lows while divergences develop.
What I want to see now is whether this rally can last more than a day or two and broaden out beyond the most beaten-down stocks. That would increase the odds that a sustainable year-end rally can develop. If it can’t, then what we’re seeing is probably just short covering with more selling still to come.
Stronger signals have come from upside breadth thrust signals than downside oversold readings. For example, returns after 10:1 upside volume days have been higher than after big downside volume days. An even stronger message would come from two 10:1 up days without an intervening 10:1 down day. It pays to wait for upside confirmation.
A follow-through day (+1% on higher d/d volume) could occur as early as this Friday, assuming Friday’s lows hold. That would be an initial step in determining a low has been made.
During corrections, my focus ultimately turns to individual stocks and market leadership. Currently, our list of potential candidates is small. A market cannot carry itself very far on the backs of counter trend rallies in broken leaders. To get bullish, we need to see more.
He's back!

Yesterday’s rally may have looked impressive, with a huge number of stocks up 10%, 20%, even 30%. But when you put those moves into perspective, it’s clear the market still has work to do.
$QQQ recovered only a relatively small portion of its recent decline and remains below a declining 10-day moving average. Most of the AI/Tech names look similar - big percentage rallies, but still badly damaged charts in well-established downtrends.
Volume on both the Nasdaq and NYSE was below the previous day. Nvidia reinstating its founder appeared to be the catalyst that ignited the rally, but the market was already heavily oversold and poised for a bounce. One day and one man are not enough to change the trend.
So the question is whether the major indexes have established a low or yesterday was simply a sharp oversold rally within an ongoing correction. Historically, some of the biggest rallies occur during bear markets.
Even if the major indexes fail to reach bear market correction percentage declines, a bear market in tech has already occurred. There are far too many stocks down 50-80%, to dismiss the declines as healthy pullbacks.
What happens from here is what matters. We need to see follow-through buying, broader participation and improving breadth. More importantly, before getting aggressive, I want to see quality stocks setting up and breaking out of sound bases - not simply broken leaders bouncing back into well-established downtrends.
Interest rates remain an obstacle. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting showed that policymakers remain concerned about inflation and that additional tightening may still be necessary.
On the positive side, we’re entering what has historically been a favorable November-December period, and the months following midterm elections have also tended to be strong, particularly during the first half of the following year.
One could argue whether those historical tailwinds will be strong enough to overcome a rising-rate environment. But I should also point out that we would never allow seasonality, cycle work - or the Fed, for that matter - to override what the market itself is actually telling us.
Those are all factors to consider, but in my world, price and volume, breadth, leadership and the action of individual stocks ultimately have the final say.
For now, the market still has to prove itself.
This is not the type of sentiment you generally see around bottoms.

The concept of a quick recovery running into overhead supply may be playing out in $SPCX. It’s starting to look similar to the Facebook analog. Time will tell.

LinkedIn was another great example. After going public in 2011, the stock suffered a huge six-week decline, then staged a powerful recovery almost all the way back to its old high. But it quickly became overwhelmed by overhead supply.

I didn’t start buying LinkedIn until the first quarter of 2013. That’s how long it took for the stock to absorb the supply, build a proper structure, and finally launch into a major move.

A great setup takes time to develop. You don't want the lowest price... you want the right price. The right price is the point at which the stock moves up into a strong price move almost immediately without hitting your stop-loss.
